Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Rotation also resists long waves in a disk Unlike a uniform three-dimensional Jeans medium, a disk is thin and rotating. A local radial compression involves Coriolis and orbital responses as well as pressure. Use a razor-thin gas disk, a local approximation, axisymmetry, and constant sound speed to examine each wavelength. κ² = 1r³d(r⁴Ω²)dr = 4Ω²+2rΩdΩdr κ is the epicyclic frequency and equals Ω for Keplerian rotation. The density Σ below is mass per disk area, not the three-dimensional density ρ. 02Obtain the gravity of a thin sheet For a surface-density wave δΣ exp(ikx), the potential outside the disk decays vertically as exp(−|kz|). Integrating Poisson’s equation across the sheet equates the jump of the vertical derivative to 4πGδΣ. δΦ(z) = δΦ(0)e−|kz| −2|k|δΦ(0) = 4πGδΣ ⇒ δΦ(0) = −2πGδΣ|k| The wavenumber dependence differs from a uniform three-dimensional medium. This expression assumes zero thickness; a finite disk thickness weakens self-gravity at short wavelengths and requires a modified kernel. 03Linearize mass and two momentum equations Use disturbances exp[i(kx−ωt)], with radial velocity perturbation u and azimuthal perturbation v. Continuity and the two momentum equations let us express surface-density and azimuthal perturbations in terms of u, then eliminate them. −iωδΣ+ikΣu = 0 −iωu−2Ωv = −ik(cs²δΣΣ+δΦ) −iωv+κ²2Ωu = 0 ω² = κ²+cs²k²−2πGΣ|k| The three terms represent rotation, pressure, and self-gravity. Rotation stabilizes long waves, while pressure stabilizes short waves. We now ask whether gravity dominates an intermediate band. 04Complete the square to obtain Q Q ≡ csκπGΣ, x ≡ |k|csκ ω²κ² = 1+x²−2xQ = (x−1Q)²+1−1Q² The minimum is 1−1/Q² at x = 1/Q. All modes have positive ω² when Q > 1. If Q < 1, a band has negative ω². At Q = 1 the mode x = 1 is neutral, with zero exponential growth rate. This is gas Q, with denominator πGΣ. A collisionless stellar disk has a different response involving its velocity distribution; a common stellar Q uses 3.36GΣ. Replacing sound speed with a dispersion is not a derivation of that result. 05The unstable band and fastest-growing mode For Q < 1, solve ω² = 0 to find the band edges and set ω = iσ inside the band. Maximum growth occurs at a finite wavelength between pressure and rotational stabilization, not at the longest possible wave. x± = 1±√(1−Q²)Q, x−<x<x+ kmax = πGΣcs², λmax = 2cs²GΣ σmaxκ = √(1Q²−1) For Q = 0.8, the unstable interval is 0.5 < x < 2, with σ = 0.75κ at x = 1.25. Applying this prediction also requires wavelengths sufficiently small compared with the disk radius for the local approximation. 06Q below one does not guarantee planet formation Compression can heat the gas and increase pressure. With slow radiative cooling, a linearly unstable disk may settle into a heated spiral or gravito-turbulent state rather than fragment. Quantities such as cooling time multiplied by Ω provide additional information about nonlinear outcomes. Cooling thresholds depend on the equation of state, resolution, irradiation, boundary conditions, and other assumptions; there is no single universal number. Use Q as a local axisymmetric linear-stability diagnostic, not a direct assignment of fragment type or mass. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For a gas disk with Q = 0.8, find the unstable interval in x = kcs/κ, the fastest-growing x, and maximum σ/κ. Show the answer and reasoning The unstable band is 0.5 < x < 2, fastest growth is at x = 1.25, and maximum σ/κ = 0.75. The endpoints are neutral. These results assume a local, axisymmetric, razor-thin gas disk and do not guarantee fragmentation into planets or stars.
